utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today is Thursday. I would like to wish Mr. Praljak a good afternoon, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Stojic, as well as the accused who are not here for various reasons, Mr. Coric, Pusic, and Mr. Prlic more specifically. I would like to greet Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer, and all the people assisting us. Ms. Nozica, on behalf of the Trial Chamber and on my own behalf, I wish to express my condolences since your sister passed away. You have all our sympathy for this ordeal that you are going through.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, and I'd like to take this opportunity to thank you and everybody else in the courtroom. Things like that, unfortunately, happen to us all, but it's always very important at times like that that the people that work with you have every sympathy and express their condolences and extend their assistance. I thank you all, Your Honours, and all my colleagues during these very difficult times for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we're going to resume. I would therefore like to ask the registrar to kindly display P06831. In the English version this is page 9.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that to come up, Your Honours, may I just give you a piece of information? Yesterday, Judge Antonetti, you said that on your web page there was a piece of information about the flu. Let me just tell you and everybody else in the courtroom that the detention unit administration informed us some ten days ago that in the hot water throughout the building they found Legionaires' disease, so spent two days impurifying the water and the pipes, but we still have the air-conditioning to be seen to. That has to be purified. So who knows. We might bring in that disease. So far we don't have any symptoms, but we have been told of the symptoms which are similar to flu symptoms. So that's what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you ever have any symptoms, please let us know and we will adjourn the hearing in that case because we will all be contaminated in this room otherwise, and everybody would have to be cured. I also heard from another accused that there was a case of Legionaires' Disease. Let's make sure that everybody is taking the appropriate measures. Mr. Praljak, you have page 9 on your screen. You have Mr. Tudjman's statement here. This is in the last paragraph on this page. On this page, Mr. Tudjman talks about the Croatian armed forces and so on, the armed forces of Croatia. I will not review the entire document, because there are a number of things in this document, but on the face of it Mr. Skender is mentioned, a number of other personalities are mentioned who were involved in the HVO. This is something you've told us already, but we wanted to be quite clear for the record. You are still saying that the officers in the army of Croatia who were part of the HVO were only officers who had volunteered but who still remained, from a military standpoint, part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I claim, Your Honour. And I know for sure that Mr. Skender, after -- well, he's a French national and lives in Corsica, and I contacted him and he expressly asked to go to the battlefront and into the HVO as a volunteer to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know about the others too. The names that are mentioned here, Roso, Kapular, and so on, they're all people who were born in Herzegovina -- or, rather, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistaken, you had intended to call Mr. Skender as a witness. I don't know if you still wish to call him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He'll come.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We will then be able to put questions of a technical nature to him. I'm sure his testimony will be very interesting. I would now like to ask the registrar to -- to display P06006. Could you display page 2, please. The registrar is telling me that there's only one page in the e-court system. In my transcript documents, I have several pages. So there's a problem. What I wanted to ask you, Mr. Praljak, is this, even if we don't have all the pages of this document -- just one moment. This is Exhibit -- this is why there's a mistake. It's P06012.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the previous document, Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, I know that Mr. Tudjman was very angry because of the mistake that General Bobetko had obviously made with respect to the way in which he issued an order, and he was extremely angry. And then he asked Susak and Bobetko to explain to him how that could have happened in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in fact already addressed this issue. I would like to have page 2, registrar, please, in the English. We have a problem for the following reason: P06012 also has a number which is P06006. So there are two exhibit numbers for the same document. If we don't see the exhibit, it doesn't matter. At some point Mr. Tudjman discusses the fact that secret agreements had been signed with the Muslims and Izetbegovic. This is on page 2 of the document. As a result, the cooperation between Muslims and Croats should be maintained. Notwithstanding the fact, Mr. Praljak, that there was a conflict between the Muslims and the HVO, Mr. Tudjman claims in this document, before the people attending the meeting on the 22nd of October, 1993, i.e., a few days before your departure, that agreements have been reached with Mr. Izetbegovic. Cooperation is therefore important when a series of events are going to take place. You yourself, did you know that secret agreements had been reached that tied Mr. Izetbegovic to Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both public and secret. There was a secret agreement and another one at the -- well, Izetbegovic wanted to sign a secret one between the parties, and in those circles the stories going round was that the Serbs would be allowed to take their part off towards Yugoslavia, and then Izetbegovic asked that a Muslim-Croatian state be formed on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it have close ties with Croatia. And then a public agreement was signed, and a secret agreement was signed in September 1993. And Mr. Tudjman on the following page there says, But in the Muslim leadership, he says, there are those who would like to continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are reading from a document, and let me again ask you umpteenth time to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour Judge Prandler. I always have this clock ticking in my head, but I will slow down. There was a public agreement and a secret agreement, and we have here a statement, and I quote Dr. Tudjman. He said as follows: "Therefore, we should bear that in mind. However, on the other hand, we must also bear in mind the fact that the Muslim leadership -- that among the Muslim leadership there are those who would like to continue offensive operations against us in Herceg-Bosna and that should be thwarted."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Prosecution in its submissions, in paragraph 232.18, states as follows -- it's very short and I'm going to ask you to comment this. He says as follows: "The president of Croatia, Tudjman, has taken a military and strategic -- strategic and tactical military decision regarding the use of aircraft in Herceg-Bosna, the disposition of both HVO and HVO troops and the awarding of pay and ranks for officers who had served in both armies while telling his own generals at the end of 1993 to make sure that they kept control of key areas in Central Bosnia." And Tudjman adds, this is on page 39 of the document and I'm reading this: "In this respect, gentlemen, we did not act well enough, and that is what I have to say as the president and supreme commander." What was said at this meeting of the 22nd of October, 1993, may testify to the fact that President Tudjman is scrutinising the military developments in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and says to the people attending the meeting that: "We have not been efficient enough." How do you interpret Mr. Tudjman's words? How are we to understand them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Constitution, the Croatian president and Croatian state is duty-bound to take care of Croats outside the Republic of Croatia, and also the destiny and fate of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the first point. The second point is this: We never -- I -- we haven't had any examples in history of somebody giving way to the other side so much on enemy territory as Franjo Tudjman gave way and gave in to Alija Izetbegovic and the Muslim leadership even while they were attacking us. Thirdly, we didn't have any planes. There were no flights, no sorties towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was not possible. Fourthly, the southern borders of Croatia were under threat and depended on the development of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They depended on the situation. And the president of the state must be interested in knowing what was happening in the neighbouring state after what had happened in Dubrovnik and after the plans of the Yugoslav People's Army and all the political games that were being played all the time. Regardless of the fact that Croatia had already been recognised and Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been recognised, there were other plots being made to resolve the whole situation, and the CSCE -- KES agreement that had been signed wasn't functioning properly. But as a normal statesman and a wise statesman, he took care of all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the registrar to display document P -- I will give the floor to my colleague. In the meantime, I will ask the registrar to display P06485.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, if one goes back to the previous page where -- we have had, namely page 2 of this document, if you look at page 3, the next page, they speak about agreements with Izetbegovic, and in the agreement here mentioned, Mr. Tudjman says it has been provided that there be this close association, a Muslim-Croatian state strongly tied to Croatia. And if that were to resolve -- dissolve, then the western part of Bosnia should be integrated into Croatia. I seem to read this as evidence of the fact that there was some interest of Croatia in having Herceg-Bosna, to put it in one word, integrated into Croatia if the friendly solution were not to work out. What is your interpretation of this sentence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've just said, Western Bosnia, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, has nothing to do with Herceg-Bosna. It's Abdic's part, and he was a man, Abdic, a Muslim who gained most of the votes at the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he didn't agree with the policy pursued by Izetbegovic. So that area, that portion that President Tudjman refers to was almost 100 percent purely Muslim. The population was almost 100 percent Muslim in the area of Kladusa, and that area was under Mr. Fikret Abdic's control. Fikret Abdic at the time talked to President Tudjman and discussed the problem of what should be done if Bosnia-Herzegovina were to disintegrate. And secondly, Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, at this same point in time, that is to say where Mr. Izetbegovic had signed this secret agreement with Tudjman about the creation of a Muslim-Croatian state on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, two days after that or one day after that he also signed an agreement with the Serbs, the one that we discussed earlier on, and now you see the situation. That's why we always look at other variants. In this agreement with the Serbs, Your Honour, Izetbegovic says, "We're going to set up two states. The Serbs will form one state," and that's why they're taking the offensive, and he says take Stolac and reach Neum in order to make two states to have complete Croatian majority under him, and then you'll be given the opportunity of a referendum in two years' time and you can go wherever you like. And of course Franjo Tudjman had to take that into account, because these were double games being played and triple games being played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let's not talk about an agreement with the Serbs of which we have no text before us. And you seem to have said that this occurred soon after the present transcript, so it's difficult that Tudjman would have taken that into account at that time. How can you explain the, for me at least, quite surprising idea that a predominantly Muslim part of Bosnia should be joined to Croatia, integral part?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a proposal put forward by Mr. Fikret Abdic. Fikret Abdic and the people around him did not want to go into a Muslim state with Izetbegovic. It wasn't President Tudjman's proposal to take over that, nor did he have any military contacts with the territory. Fikret Abdic came to Zagreb and put a solution of that type on the table in front of President Tudjman should Bosnia-Herzegovina fall apart. And Franjo Tudjman quite simply would have had to go through all the parliamentary procedure and the whole of the Croatian people would have had to state their views. So this is Fikret Abdic coming to Tudjman, saying, "I don't want to join up with a Muslim state. I would rather merge with a Croatian state." I mean as an idea, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. Tudjman speaks of an agreement, "We have an agreement with Mr. Abdic." So he must also have agreed to it, "tocno"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Well, I don't know. If you have three cantons in Switzerland, Unterwalden, Shwyz, and the third one, they also have an agreement to unite. It's a proposal like any other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You missed my point. You missed my point. You said it was Abdic. Abdic wanted, Abdic wanted, but Tudjman seems also to have wanted because otherwise there would not have been an agreement. That's all I'm saying. It's rather obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tudjman did agree, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And just one more sentence if I may. They were supposed to be separate. It wasn't a fact that they would come in to the state of Croatia. They asked to be autonomous and a canton which in one way or another would be conjoined. There was a lot of discussion about this. It's not very -- it's not a simple matter taking over territory or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It says here an integral part and whatever that may be or mean, I don't think it's useful to discuss that further. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was a certain amount of misunderstanding perhaps due to the transcript or perhaps due to a different understanding on the word "agreement," "sporazum," because Mr. Praljak clearly said that this was a hypothetical, Abdic's hypothetical proposal, what if, or if, and the word that was used, "sporazum," in colloquial Croatian, and we're dealing with colloquial Croatian, does not mean a legally binding document with a signature. It means just agreement or consent. So it's not agreement in a legally binding document sense, not even proposed and not signed. That's not it. It's just sort of in the spirit of the language consent, thinking the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. Actually, I had understood it in this sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we will have opportunity to review Mr. Abdic's position when we see the presidential transcripts. Mr. Praljak, I'm asking you to be very concise when you answer, because otherwise -- well, let me tell you what's going to happen. I hope I will finish my questions on Monday, and one will say that Judge Antonetti has spent five days with General Praljak and 20 hours. I won't, in fact, have had 20 hours. I may have put two hours questions worth of time, but you would have had 18 hours, and those 20 hours will be my hours. Try and be as concise as you possibly can, because otherwise those will be counted on my time. I know that you are making a lot of effort, but, General Praljak, let's look at page 29 of the document. Registrar, please, page 29 of this document. We're waiting for the page to be displayed. The Prosecutor says in 232.19 of its brief that Mr. Tudjman gave orders to the HV HVO and that in July 1993 he told Bobetko and Roso to send Croatian troops to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in doing so to reward the units and officers with higher-level designations and ranks. And this is on page 29 of the document. Let me quote. I don't know whether this is now visible on our screens. Tudjman said this: "For psychological reasons, you'll give them ranks. Politically this is needed, as well as capable military commanders and political people." In saying so -- or he said this to Bobetko and Roso. Now, I'm interested in this: Apart from the military aspect, he seems to give instructions for politicians or political people to be put into places. He wants competent political people. This is written in black and white. You can see that yourself. So how do you read this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no politicians here. He says for political reasons. He mentions military commanders and political people. I don't know. I've never seen political people anywhere else. But let me tell you this: There were a lot of people in Herzegovina, in the Croatian leadership, including Skegro, Ramljak, Dr., who occasionally had to go there to assist, and he and President Tudjman is talking about volunteers, and volunteers would not want to go into war if you did not reward them. Those were volunteers from the Croatian army. And after all this talk, they managed to gather 400 of them, volunteers, and I sell -- I say that with a lot of reliability. I know what I'm saying. And he says here a -- form companies. A Croatian company was always less than a hundred men, and then you call it a battalion. And then you call your brigade -- battalions brigades, which creates a lot of confusion. A company's called a battalion, a battalion is called a brigade, and when you put all of them together, you can count less than 400 people in all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's look at document P6675.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 6575.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 18. Paragraph 232.20. This is what the Prosecutor said: "Tudjman ordered the military to transfer what remains of the troops from Vares to Kiseljak and to push through to Busovaca." Tudjman continues and says this, this is to be seen on page 18: "You know that I sent a new commander, and I ordered that new volunteers be sent in order to defend the Vitez line." So, General Praljak, Mr. Tudjman is very interested in the military situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina since he himself says that he sent a new commander and has ordered that new volunteers be sent. How do you interpret this sentence? Can we draw the conclusion that Mr. Tudjman is the one that directs and controls everything, or is it that he's trying to be a little -- he adds on to what is really happening?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. -- if Mr. Tudjman had been in control of -- over everything, then as the supreme commander he would have issued an order to the 1st, 2nd, or the 3rd Guards Brigade, and he would have ordered them go there. He did not do that because he was not allowed to do that. He was prohibited from doing so by the Constitution. He -- 400 volunteers were gathered on a promise of somewhat higher salary and promotion, and with -- after all the promises he managed to gather only 400 of them. Tudjman was aware, based on the agreement that I spoke about, that if the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina defeated the HVO, then Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina would no longer be able to exercise any of their rights because there would be no rights to speak of. 14 So he is not talking about taking over territories but joining up the line 15 that was lost between Kiseljak and Busovaca where the Croats represent the 16 majority, and joining up the two enclaves that remained isolated was a task that was given to General Petkovic while I was still the commander down there. He was going to try to do that but he did not have enough strength to do so. We never had enough troops to do so and this was never accomplished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had planned now to show you documents, but we have addressed the documents already, but my fellow Judge wants to say something. Let me finish this sentence. I wanted to submit four documents. I'm going to give you the numbers: P00136. It is your appointment by Mr. Susak to the position of vice-minister or assistant minister for defence. I suppose you're not going to challenge this document. Then P00465 in which President Tudjman appointed you to the council for defence. P03683. This is your appointment to the position of HVO commander. And P05796, in which Mr. Petkovic is appointed commander -- deputy commander of the HVO. We've seen these documents already, so I guess you will not have any remarks. I just have a minor question, and it is this one: When you joined the Council for National Defence, which was a very important council, why were you appointed to it? Was it because you were friends with Susak, or was it the fact that you applied against -- were a candidate against Tudjman, or was it because you were very competent? Why were you chosen and appointed, because we know that there were 14 members in this council. It was really the very best among the best.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was competent, educated. I was intelligent, handsome, young, charming. That's why. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, it was not Susak who appointed me as assistant. It was Franjo Tudjman. It was not Susak who appointed assistant ministers, it was Franjo Tudjman himself. And we're talking about document P00136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. I can see Mr. Tudjman's signature, indeed. But I believe that Judge Trechsel had a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petkovic also wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to check whether you mentioned P05796 as the document in which Petkovic was appointed as deputy. That's the way I understood what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. P05796 is a document that shows that Mr. Petkovic is the assistant to the HR HB OS commander. We can call up the document. Please, Mr. Registrar, call up P05796.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can see the document. However, the interpretation I received implied that this is the document on my appointment, whereas it is not. There is another document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody can see this document now, and you are the deputy. Yes, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the passage we had a moment ago at page 18 of 59 where Tudjman says to Mr. Prlic and the other attendants: "You know that I sent a new commander and ordered that new volunteers be sent to defend the Vitez line." And your reaction, Mr. Praljak, was to say that is not possible because the Constitution does not allow this, if I have understood correctly. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. I said the following: This is precisely about the -- Dr. Franjo Tudjman's limitations. If it was true that Franjo Tudjman was omnipotent and that he could violate the Constitution, he would have issued an order and sent Croatian brigades to fight down there. He would not have implored people to go there as volunteers. He would not have issued them promises if they decided to go and fight. People didn't gladly go to war, not even soldiers. In Croatia he was in a position to issue orders that had to be obeyed. However, under the Constitution of Croatia, he could not send the regular Croatian army to fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and indeed he never did that. That's why all the time we're talking about volunteers and defence. To defend the line in Vitez meant that the BH Army wanted to take that line. There's no reference to attacks or taking territories. The only reference that's made ever is to defend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm sorry, I'm not through with this. I don't know where you take attack. Who spoke about attack? Have I spoken about attack? I have not. You're not answering the question. Please hold it. Hold it. Did Mr. Tudjman send a new commander as he says? He says, "I," he says to the attendants, "You know that I sent a new commander." Is he lying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody lies. This is not the truth. He's using the word in the colloquial terms. Roso volunteered. Mate Boban appointed Roso and Tudjman, of course, and all of that tried to find somebody from the Croatian army to would down there so Tudjman is not lying, but it is not that he sent him. He it's just a turn of the phrase. I found somebody and I've sent him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yesterday or the day before you have told us that the war was mainly defined by lies in writing. So if you say nobody lies today, there's a rather gross contradiction in that, but I think it's more a matter of speech. To order volunteers, that's what he says. How logical is it to order volunteers? Are people who you ordered to go somewhere volunteers who do not want to go, as you told us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, I can't understand your logic. It's -- it's totally alien to me. I apologise. Hold on a moment. Let me answer your question, sir. I'm talking about a war, about erroneous reports. When it comes to the number of dead on the other side in terms of what had been done and so on and so forth. Here Franjo Tudjman is talking to his team of his most intimate associates, and he's very open when he speaks to them. And when you're looking for volunteers, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, then you raise the level of incentive, as it were. And if you can't find somebody who wants to go and do -- and swim, then you tell them, "Okay. I'm offering a thousand euros for somebody to go swimming, or 2.000 euros." So you are narrowing down the problem to a certain measure in order to resolve the problem. So Franjo Tudjman wants to help. He says yes, volunteers, but there will be no force, and it will be -- it will not be the Croatian army. And he raises the level of incentive, and once the level of incentive was raised enough, 400 people gathered as volunteers to go down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I have the answer that you have given in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, before we move on to the so-called presidential transcripts which I will break down into two parts, there will be 11 transcripts that I will address before I move on to other transcripts. I hope your answers will be brief so that I can ask you many questions. Let me finish with one final question, because Ms. Nozica mentioned this. It is about the fact that you knew -- or what you knew of Mr. Stojic as part of the joint criminal enterprise, because together with you we looked at all the names in the indictment, and we postponed the issue of Mr. Stojic until Ms. Nozica was back, and now that she's back I can revisit the issue regarding Mr. Stojic, but I'll do it along the same plan as the one I used for all the other people. You knew Mr. Stojic, and more exactly, when did you get to know him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1992, in Grude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prior to April 1992, had you heard of him or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What were the circumstances of you meeting him in Grude in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went down there to be -- to be a commander. We know that. And on that day, the Serbs were attacking Kupres in order to take it. The situation was bad, the circumstances were bad. I met him under very adverse circumstances for the HVO and the Croatian people, and it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was his position when you met him precisely?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you discuss with him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I know that he did something in the HVO logistics, and then I got to know him through the documents that we've seen during the talks with the Tuzla Corps as regards the weapons, some joint orders to the effect of spending New Years Eve with the men on the front line, with regard to the setting up military police check-points. So before the day when I arrived as commander, we met, but I don't know how many times. Five, six. You can see it in the documents. There are documents that -- that show that. And we would always meet to discuss a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you met him and discussed with him, how did he come across? What was your impression of him? How did you see and feel him at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perceived him as a diligent, passionate man who simply pursued the same policy as everybody else, and that was the policy which is demonstrated by the documents and exactly the one that I claim that it was with regard to the position of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was a normal, passionate, hard-working person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he someone who had sort of very specific political views or was he part of the general frame of mind of Croats living in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or did he insist on specific topics that may have struck you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, nothing. He simply advocated the same thing all of us did, and that was how to avoid a conflict with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He armed that army together with the rest of us, as you could have already seen. He tried to get along with everybody, and his big problem was the supply of all the units and how to provide them with everything that they should have had. The biggest problem that I knew and that I discussed with him -- actually, there were two problems. The first one was how to raise the level of the HVO supplies so that they could fight and also the problem of mobilisation, which did not function at all. And those two problems were enough, and I know that from our conversations. Those two problems were really taking a toll on him and on me. On two occasions he fainted in front of my very eyes, and I know that once this was on 15th of August, 1993. I know that for a fact. He was exhausted, it was hot, and he was faced with a problem which was that the BiH army near Blagaj almost had broken the line towards the southern parts -- part of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me get into the details. You know that Mr. Stojic was the chief of the defence department and later on minister for defence. From July to November what were your relations to the minister for defence? Were you in a situation of subordination to him, or was it another type of relation, but he was not your chief, your chief being Mate Boban? Could you define the nature and type of relations between you, HVO commander, and the minister for defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 24th of July until the 9th of November Bruno Stojic was the head of the defence department. And in that part, in that segment, due to the war operations we did not meet on too many occasions. Towards the end of my tour of duty we met a few more times. I would go to his house to take a bath. His mother was my hostess. And second of all, he was not my superior. My superior was Mate Boban. And thirdly, in part the army was part of the defence department. And let me not go over the same grounds again. We've already spoken about that a dozen of times. The defence department was to take care of boots, hats, ammunition, everything that a military needs to be efficient. He was not in charge of mobilisation, but that was our common problem. I'm talking about municipal bodies that should have been in charge of that. Then we also have the problem of how to supply Central Bosnia. Those were the problems that he was faced with all the time, and I obviously would come to him with my requests which he could not meet. For example, I would come and go and ask for the money for the troops. Money was always a problem, and all the other problems stemmed from that problem, the problem of money. Let me not go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you said something that struck me as very important and very interesting. When you were speaking about the way the Republic of Croatia functioned. Speaking about Mr. Bobetko, you said of him that he was an elderly man who defended this idea that as a senior officer of the former JNA it was the Main Staff that had to control and direct and not the Ministry for Defence, whilst in the Republic of Croatia there were some people who thought that it was the Ministry for Defence that had to direct the Main Staff as it does happen in many democratic countries. So it was a major political debate inside the country. Did you have this discussion inside the HVO? Did Mr. Stojic as minister for defence have any ambitions or claims to direct the Main Staff or did he just stay on the sideline, and did he let the Main Staff, you in this case, did he let them do whatever they had to do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic did not show any desire to in operative terms to head the army vis-a-vis me, and nobody in Croatia wanted the defence to be above the Main Staff, but the Main Staff should not be above the defence ministry. So there's a difference there, how far the army leans on the Ministry of Defence and all its departments, but command goes, Mate Boban, Slobodan Praljak, Milivoj Petkovic from the president downwards. Now, whether it's Tus or Bobetko or whoever, but Gojko Susak was in charge of seeing that the SIS was doing its job, that the military police was doing its job, that the services for care and welfare should do their job and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In November you left your position, and you told us why. We know that a few days later Mr. Stojic --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting but I see that something very important was not recorded. On page 23, lines 2 and 3. Mr. Praljak, before he started enumerating the names, Mr. Tudjman, Susak, said "in Croatia." He compared Croatia. So the keyword is "in Croatia." Otherwise, we don't know who, what, and where Mr. Susak had to exert control. So I think he explained what happened first and then said "in Croatia." That has been omitted from the transcript, and Mr. Praljak could put me right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in the -- in Croatia operative command went from Tudjman, then the Chief of the Main Staff, Tus or Bobetko or some third person, and then horizontally to the side you have the Ministry of Defence led by Gojko Susak, and that provided support, if I can use just that one word, to the HVO in Herceg-Bosna. And then you have Mate Boban, in operative terms Slobodan Praljak, Petkovic, Tole and so on, whereas Bruno Stojic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we know all this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A correction to the transcript. I think it was Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic who had taken the floor, not Ms. Tomanovic. This is no value judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, on the 13th [as interpreted] of December, 1993, Mr. Stojic is appointed head of the office in charge of production and selling of weapons and military equipment. This is on the 16th of December to be precise. A few weeks before that, he was minister of defence, and now all of a sudden he heads this office or bureau. How do you interpret this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, normal. It's normal. In those times that was quite normal, Judge Antonetti. Those times didn't mean that you would develop in your career. That's what happened. A new team turned up, and you would go to quite a different place. If he was an economist and good organiser, why wouldn't he take over that position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have read a lot and studied a lot of things. I believe -- I think you also did an internship in the Netherlands. I think you spent a short time in the army in the Netherlands. I seem to remember reading something about this. I may be mistaken. I don't know. As far as your knowledge of ministers of defence is concerned worldwide, I mean, is it normal for someone in that position to find himself or herself demoted, or was this specific to the Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is customary. I can quote the example of the great General Schwarzkopf, for example, who went through the Desert Storm and then no longer wanted to work for the salary that he was given in the army and then decided to join a private company, or McNamara, the famous McNamara, if you will. I'm sure that people of our age will remember that. He was an excellent US minister of defence and then joined up with a private company. For a far higher salary, of course, but a far lower position. So I don't know whether Mr. Stojic profited in terms of money, but that is customary that you go to the economy or commerce when you conclude your work in that position and I can quote other examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This office in charge of production and selling of weapons, did this operate like a private company?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't suppose so, no. Certainly not. But the selling -- well, it wasn't a private company because everything had been mobilised. He has to have the army pay, because he has to buy the semi-manufacturers and the production materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now turn to a series of documents. The first one is P00147. I would like us to turn to pages 23 and 24. This is a meeting which takes place on the 6th of April, 1992. Mr. Susak, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Munivrana [phoen], Sarinic, and Kikari [phoen] are present, and other people also. Lucic. General Praljak, you're going to take the floor. As you can see on the screen, this is what you said, and you said that the success or failure of military actions entails the responsibility of the commanders. This is on page 23. And you suggest conducting an investigation into those actions that failed. This is on page 24. Do you remember having said this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You seem to be saying that the commanders are responsible for military operations.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. There are military operations. Well, it's difficult without going into specifics. Yes. Once we perform an analysis, we can say whether a military commander led the operation well but still lost because of the supremacy of the enemy and so on and so forth, but in this particular case there were two actions under way taken by General Gorinsek who had completed the greatest military schools within the Yugoslav People's Army. And let me just say that I took part in the commission that investigated this, together with Generals Tus and Bobetko, and I asked that he be replaced and he was indeed replaced. And then there was another action across the Sava River near where I was, whereas the commanders of the companies stayed on one side and allowed the troops to go ahead on the other, and that is why -- that is untenable, and that's why I ask that an inquiry be undertaken and that there be a selection in the Croatian army. Those are my positions and I stand by them today, quite literally word-for-word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at the next document which is P00353. Page 24. General Praljak, before the attendees at this meeting, you were going to say that you spent seven days in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the military situation was extremely chaotic, that there were a number of casualties, and the units were laying the blame at each other's door. You are describing this in a rather worrying way. This is a military situation in July and August of 1998.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, we're dealing with Posavina here. I was in Posavina. Perhaps two days more than seven days, but anyway, this is Posavina. The situation was indeed catastrophic. The commanders did not have or hardly had any information. They were poorly informed about what was happening on the ground precisely because they were conveying this basic idea, because they were mostly from the JNA, that they were 100 kilometres from the front line, and then they should draw on maps where the brigades were, the position of the brigades. And when you went to the spot, you would see that there were no battalions, no brigades, and that the whole situation was very bad and that's why Posavina ultimately fell. It was lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this detail. Let's have a look at page 31 which I would like to say is a page that has not been admitted so far.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could you ask General Praljak an additional question, say whether the Main Staff of the HVO was in commander of Posavina at that time or whether somebody else was in command, because that's very important. Who commanded that army in Posavina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Main Staff of the HVO was not in command at that time, not in command of Posavina. Posavina had a separate command in Bosanski Brod, and then in Slavonski Brod, and then for that whole area of the defence of Croatia and Posavina, the command was in Djakovo led by General Stipetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was General Stipetic --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was supposed to coordinate all the efforts of the HVO and Croatian assistance and the assistance of the Croatian army, and then underneath him the command that was in Slavonski Brod and then Bosanski Brod, but they all did their job very badly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 31 it's at the top -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: On the latter -- on the latter point, Mr. Praljak. Would that mean that General Stipetic was immediately under the command of Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So who -- who did he have to answer to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, he answered to the forces of Bosanska Posavina of the HVO and coordination. Well, quite simply Boban was at a different end all together and he had no communication. It's a ten-hour drive. No telephones, no communication whatsoever. It was a completely separate battlefront in which part of Bosanska Posavina was defending itself, that is to say the Serbs -- or, rather, the Croats and the Muslims, but Croatia was under threat, and that's why Stipetic was supposed to coordinate the overall effort, logistically and to help the HVO to defend themselves and the volunteers there, too, and this didn't function, and that's why everything fell through in October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did he ever file, to your knowledge, a report on his work there and to whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the fall of Posavina -- well, now, once again I have to expand my answer. The fall of Posavina coincided with the withdrawal of the Serb and Montenegrin forces from Prevlaka, and Franjo Tudjman then launched -- or, rather, it was said that Franjo Tudjman had made an agreement to give -- cede Posavina for the Prevlaka, and then Dr. Tudjman ordered an investigation to be carried out, a military inquiry, and to investigate the service within the police to see how the fall of Bosanska Posavina came about. I was a member of the commission representing the military which investigated, and there were two reports written about that, and if you would like, I can supply them here. And I even published some of those findings in the form of a book. So anybody who is interested in reading about this, about the investigation and inquiry, I can provide them with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you -- could you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when the investigation was carried out? Immediately after the fall of Bosanska Posavina. Instructions were given that this should be investigated at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to help out with the record. On page 28, lines 15, 16, where the general started to explain the events in Posavina and it says here that it was the Croats and Muslims defending themselves against the Serbs, but the sentence was left in the air. I don't think the general formulated it properly. Perhaps this was not reflected in the interpretation, so it's not quite clear although we can interpret it properly, but perhaps the general could tell us who was fighting in Posavina, which sides were fighting against each other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 101st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th. These were all brigades of the HVO, and they were composed of Croats and Muslims. HVO brigades in Posavina. They were doing the fighting. And everything else was coordination. And interpreters, please refrain from any comments. I have had enough of your comments. You should do your work and not talk about the poor Defence counsel or whatever words and phrases you use. You should be ashamed of yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the problem, Mr. Praljak? What did you hear in your headphones?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard, Your Honour, was this: There was a comment made to what the Defence counsel said, or, rather, a comment from the booth, because they weren't attentive enough and their microphone was left on, and they uttered the following sentence, and I quote: "Well, this Defence counsel is one sorry man." So as far as the interpreters are concerned, Mr. Kovacic, you are one sorry man. Now, that -- those interpreters should be replaced. Now, you see Judge Trechsel, you see what this looks like when friends are working amongst themselves and you're asking questions? The army works that way too. Everybody covers everybody else. Well, they did it so that -- now, they say well, never mind, don't go on. Well, that was the same situation in the HVO. Some commanders that committed evil deeds covered each other. They covered each other, and everybody ends up covering each other, whereas I'm sitting here in this seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I'm not covering anyone.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I wasn't referring to you, Your Honours. Don't misunderstand me. I just said what the situation was like in society generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar of this Tribunal is always very attentive and checks the transcript. Management will know what has happened. There will be an in-house inquiry, and I will let you know what the outcome of it is. Let me get back to the document. I have displayed page 31, and before that we should see page 30, but we're not going to waste any time. Mr. Tudjman is talking about a thousand Mujahedin, and he says that, "They are against us, and this situation is chaotic." And at that point you step in and you say: "Mr. President, I've given a clear ethnic card to Mr. Cermak." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this ethnic card you gave Colonel Cermak at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided him with the ethnic map of Bosanska Posavina; that is to say, the region we're discussing, and I said to him, Look you have the Croats and the Muslims who are in the majority there, not to take it municipality by municipality, and that can be defended with good fortification, good artillery support and so on. Unfortunately, there were no fortifications nor did they cooperate amongst themselves and there was a domino effect and everything toppled, the whole area toppled, and I was putting proposals here as to how the situation could be dealt with but you're not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction ethnic map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I was going to say, I think the word "carte" in French came into the transcript as "card" in English, but I think the reference in the transcript is to map instead of card.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This had to do with the ethnic composition in the Posavina. Mr. Cermak at the time, well, what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It says they went too far. I say they went too far where the Serbs have the majority. So it's not -- the object is not to take control but it is defence, and Mr. Cermak was the main logistics man of the HV, yes, the main logistics man of the Croatian army at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's look document P466, page 17. This is a document we've seen already. There we have it. You have already told us that you'd had a lot of talks with Mr. Tudjman and other people, and you told us that as far as you were concerned, the conflict would be inevitable. This is what I read here, and these are your own words. You say: "It will be difficult to prevent a war between the Croats and the Muslims. It is on the brink of starting, if you like." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something you say on the 11th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, the Prozor events had not taken place yet.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th? What was the date? On the 11th of September? The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as you know, before Prozor - but I believe I've put the question to other witnesses already - had there been any skirmishes or problems between the various factions which bore no serious consequences. As far as you no, where there any tensions, any shots, any fights, anything?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only minor ones, not -- not too much. But let me say very loud and clear, and we'll see who understands me. Your Honours, I'm a good, an excellent analyst of the current situation, and I have this ability to forecast, to see how things will develop in the near future. A conflict doesn't arise from skirmishes or tensions but from the foundations of a war. It is born in the minds of the sides that would eventually be involved. The way the Muslims thought about themselves, about the state they would have, had to lead into conflict. I knew that, and I repeated that on the 13th of January to the French delegation and so on and so forth. In those terms, I am good. I'm among the best if not the best in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't help noticing, I'm sure, General Praljak, that -- that you say that it will be very difficult to prevent this war, and President Tudjman seemingly interrupts you and says to you: "Let us continue." And then he discusses another topic. How can you explain the fact that Mr. Tudjman avoided this question by wanting to move on to another topic? Did he not want to listen to the analysis you were making? Was he ill at ease? How can you explain the fact that he did not want to discuss this matter with you, because in a number of other documents he listened carefully to you. This is something which is mentioned in another -- in a number of documents. Why did he not want to listen to you in this case? Was this due to the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that respect, I was pessimistic, although I thought I was only realistic, and Mr. Tudjman, on the other hand, was also realistic but optimistic at the same time. Up to the month of May, I employed all my strength to prevent the war, but then I saw that -- this before as I told to Clausewitz or as Clausewitz said, originated from the very depth of the thoughts that prevailed in the territory. Tudjman said the Muslims cannot attack us. They are being attacked by the Serbs. How can they do that? And my realistic thought leaned on pessimistic and his leaned on optimistic. In my experience the situation on the ground develops even in a more adverse way than you ever envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now look at document P00524. Page 17. This is a meeting held on the 26th of September, 1992. Several attendees are there. There's Mr. Mesic, Mr. Lucic, Mr. Sarinic, you yourself, and Mr. Susak, and as well as, of course, the president. You say this on page 17: You say that refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina should be accepted in Croatia and then sent to the borders and then, seemingly, it doesn't matter. What did you mean to say regarding the refugees?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to say this: First of all, I start by saying -- and if I can just read one sentence to you. Muslim refugees in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and I had reliable information about all that along private and any other lines. In Croatia they talk about Bosnia and Herzegovina as the only country they had. They -- nobody even mentioned the HZ HB. That was the foundation that would lead to all the problems that appeared later on. I would also like to say that this could also be internationalised as a problem and say that we are at a war. According to the rules of the International Red Cross, any refugees are sent to the neighbouring peaceful state. In Croatia there was still war around Sisak. Sisak was being bombed. And I said why don't we send refugees to France, for example, and show the scope of the problem to France? I once had an argument about -- about that with Prime Minister Greguric about Croatian refugees. Nobody cared about our problems. Our population was 4 million, and we had 800.000 refugees. My view was that we should let the world know how big a problem we were facing. The way I saw it was let's send them to the border to show the world what kind of a problem we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let me ask you a very important question. You have just said that there were about 4 million inhabitants in our country, you said in the Republic of Croatia. You said there were 800.000 refugees. Approximately how many -- among this figure of 800.000 refugees, how many Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One-half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four hundred thousand, you say. Let's say that there were about 10 percent of Muslims compared to the overall Croatian population. The fact that 10 percent of Muslims are going to settle down in the Republic of Croatia, is that a fact that may cause -- or a shift in the ethnic balance in some municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it could not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a tricky question. There's no trap, no pitfall. I never ask tricky questions. I just want to ascertain whether the fact that 10 percent of people come into the country may change some ethnic balance.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This could not happen in Croatia because they did not become Croatian citizens. They knew that they could not remain living in Croatia. But there were other problems, a number of other problems. They behaved as if they were not refugees. They had all sorts of requests. For example, they wanted to have a ferry between the mainland and the island that had never had a ferry. They saw themselves as the citizens of Yugoslavia and that they should have whatever they wanted. That was the first problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'm asking you this question as part of the joint criminal enterprise. If we take the Prosecution case that ethnic balance had to be changed in Herzegovina so that Croats would be in a majority situation, therefore that through ethnic cleansing Muslims have to be expelled, but then the Muslims would go to Croatia. Are they not going to cause problems in Croatia? So one believes one has solved a problem in Herzegovina, but another problem is being created in the Republic of Croatia. I'm seeking some logical links here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no logic there at all. If I'm in Mostar and if I expel 13 Muslims from there to my weekend cottage and I pay their bills for them, what kind of an ethnic cleansing can this be. Your Honour, in -- in Herzegovina there were 90 percent Croats before the war. There's no way you can change the ethnic composition there. They were all Croats. And let me just tell you this: If Muslims in 1993 had won a military victory, do you know what was happening in Dalmatian hotels in Croatia? Muslim refugees celebrated the victories of their army over the Croatian army [as interpreted], and it happened all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that there were around 400.000 Muslim refugees. What about the dates? When did these 400.000 refugees arrive? Was it in 1992, 1993, or 1991? Did they come at specific days or did their -- was their arrival spread over several years?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]. Page 37, line 12, the general said victories over the HVO. In the transcript I read the Croatian army. It should read the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, out of the 400.000 refugees, did they arrive continuously or in spurts? Did they arrive at one point in time and then not? We have documents, but I'm not here to testify in your stead, so please answer this question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were arriving all the time in waves. There was a constant influx with some peaks in 1992 after a very strong attack by the Serbs, then another one in 1993. Gradually some left to live in third countries, but they were replaced by new ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's look at P01622. Page 36 first. We have Tudjman speaking here towards the middle. Can you see the middle of this page? He says that they're going to send Praljak again -- Praljak again to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Susak will then speak in order to say that Praljak will return to Bosnia and Herzegovina on Thursday where he stayed permanently, and Susak said that he was not withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina but that he returned voluntarily to Croatia in order to attend a seminar in the Netherlands. This is the reason why I mentioned this time you spent in the Netherlands earlier on. All this is to be found only pages 36 to 42. Do you remember attending a seminar in the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a seminar in the Netherlands. I was supposed to attend it, but I was replaced by somebody else. I was somewhere else. In Germany, in a NATO military exercise, I believe. I'm a bit confused about the dates, and without appropriate documents I can't remember the events, the travel. There was so much, and it is very difficult for me to list all those chronologically without the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand well, you went abroad every now and then. You said that there was a NATO exercise in Germany?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you knew how the armies of the European Union or the NATO armies would operate.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- yes, very well. From the moment when Charles de Gaulle left NATO, I know quite a lot about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You were a waiter in Germany. Did you learn German? Do you speak German?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's close to time for a break, close to 4.00. You know we have only have one break today. Let us look at P01739. Pages 26 and 27, please. We can see here that Mr. Susak and Mr. Izetbegovic speak about you. On page 26, Susak says that you are in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tudjman is going to say that Praljak thought that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina - this is on page 27 - more -- were -- or that the Muslims were being wrung a little by Croats, and then somebody says that he is going to try and speak to Praljak on the next day. Do you remember having had a meeting following this meeting on the next day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It says here that I said to President Tudjman not that they ill-treated Muslims but that Croats did some things wrong vis-a-vis Muslims. There were minor wrong-doings. And President Izetbegovic did not call me, but although I -- but never mind. Forget that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had he called you to speak about this, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time I was doing my utmost to prevent any conflicts. In the month of March I went to Central Bosnia. I spoke to Izetbegovic. I'd spoken to Jaganjac before that, and I asked Izetbegovic to assign two prominent politicians to work with me, and I say here under the oath that Izetbegovic was playing a double game. He deceived Tudjman, the Croats, everybody. Everybody -- everything indicated that he would attack us. We were pissing blood to prevent conflict and he, all the while together with Halilovic, did everything he could to make this conflict happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This meeting between Tudjman and Izetbegovic took place on the 27th of March, 1993. So on that day you were not yet the HVO commander, but apparently Mr. Izetbegovic knew that you had a part to play because he spoke about you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I was not commander. And as for Mr. Izetbegovic, from the month of June or maybe May 1992, he knew everything about my policy, my role and the efforts that I was investing. He was well informed about everything, and I had a long conversation with him in Mostar. He was aware of all of my views and positions. There's no doubt whatsoever about that. He knew about the significance, the role, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's first move to private session for a few moments. We have a decision to hand down.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're back in open session, and we're now going to look at document -- at Exhibit P03112, page 54. As you can see on page 54, Mr. Tudjman had a long speech. He told Bobetko and Susak to go and meet with the leaders -- with the Herceg-Bosna leaders. Among the leaders we find General Praljak, Mr. Petkovic, Ambassador Sancevic, Boban, and Prlic. In order to speak about the involvement of Croatia in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Very well. Mr. Praljak, I'm trying to see whether you attended the meeting that took place on the 2nd of July, 1993, from 9.00 until 10.50 in the evening. There is Mesic, Manolic, Radic, and other attendees, but you didn't seem -- you don't seem to have been there. We can't see your name. We see Mr. Sanader was there, and unless I'm mistaken he's currently a prime minister of the country. You didn't attend the meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was this request made by Mr. Tudjman who had invited Bobetko and Susak to go and meet with you. Was there any follow-up to that? Did you meet with them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I did not meet with them with this regard. I don't think so, no. I'm sure that I did not meet with Bobetko, and I'm not sure whether I had a meeting with Susak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did President Tudjman, in early July, think it was necessary to send his minister, Susak, and General Bobetko to meet with the Herceg-Bosna leaders? Was it such a critical situation that you had to have a meeting straight away?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was after the 30th when there was an all-out attack by the BH Army in Mostar and elsewhere. And Mr. Tudjman was simply concerned. He was worried and said that steps should be taken for us to protect ourselves in the territorial sense and with respect to the economy. But he says that the people over there should not be left to their own devices, which means he's taking care of them. And when he says "those people," the people in another state, that they should be helped out so that they don't feel alone, left to their own devices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is directly connected to the consequences of the BH Army attack end of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And with the continuation of the operations in Central Bosnia and Bugojno. I don't know what date this is. What's the date of this? 3rd of July. So then that's after Mostar, and there were attacks in Central Bosnia directly linked to the attack launched by the BH Army, an all-out open attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the next document, P3467. Page -- pages 11, 16, and 17. This meeting was held on the 15th of July, 1993, at 8.25 p.m., Granic, Susak, Bobetko, Sarinic, Sacic, and Zounzak [phoen] are attending. You were not attending the meeting, and Valentic reminded Tudjman that officially speaking, Praljak was still his assistant, and he suggested that the situation should be changed. This is to be found on page 16. You can see this on page 16.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm looking at a different page, not the one you're referring to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now we've got page 16 on the screen. Look at what Nikica Valentic said. Who is this man, Nikica Valentic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the government of Republic of Croatia at that time. And I wasn't his assistant. He had his ministers, and I don't know how he came to know that, but probably he was wrongly informed. I had already been relieved of my duties. Now, who provided him with this information, how he knew whether I was assistant defence minister, whatever, I don't know, because as the prime minister, I don't know how he came to hear of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 17 -- let's have page 17. The next page. Apparently it's difficult to understand why Mr. Valentic would like Mr. Tudjman to relieve you of your duties only to appoint you -- or reappoint you. What was the problem?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the problem was that Mr. Valentic quite obviously did not know. Well, he thought that I was on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the information he received, and that's true. And since there were objections all the time based on poor information about meddling and interference, he did not know that I had been replaced and relieved of my duties. He says, "Relieve him if he's down there," and probably somebody said to him, "Well, Praljak is at the same time --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's now have P05080. Pages 18 to 20. This meeting was held on the 15th of September, 1993. It was presided over by Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Boban was present, too, together with other people.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page -- on pages 18 to 20 -- well, page 20, more exactly, you spoke, Mr. Praljak, and you claim that although Croatian units depended on cooperation with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that, Your Honour? I can't find it. And the interpretation that I received, then that isn't correct, because on the previous page I was speaking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 19.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the situation and the Muslim offensive, and I'm saying that it won't bear fruit. We already knew that at the time, that it would not. And I go on to say that relations between the Serbs and the Croats have advanced, progressed, and I say that whole units depend on cooperation with the Serbs, in Zepce and Kiseljak specifically. So Zepce and Kiseljak, as far as we were concerned, were under a total siege, under a total encirclement, and go on to say that it will -- we'll find it difficult to supply Vares given the situation because that was under an encirclement too. Vitez was also under siege as was Busovaca or, rather, Kiseljak, and Vares and Zepce, and it is correct, Your Honour, that as far as Zepce's concerned, and Kiseljak, we supplied them both across the territory held by the Army of Republika Srpska, because that was the only way of avoiding having the Muslims do there what they did in Vares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what it is in your language, because in English we have "relations." What did you say in your language? Did you speak about relations or cooperation? What is the exact word that you used in your own language?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Odnosi," economic relations. We would pay them in -- by way of fuel in order for them to allow us to cross their territory taking MTS to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, General. We're now looking at the English version, and we see more specifically at a military level. So we're not talking about economic relations here, are we?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about a military level. I don't think we should attach anything to this sentence, because I don't know what the political attitude was. Whether Prlic did anything with them, I really don't know. What I'm saying is that we had relations with them, and they were precisely defined. We never had a joint operation or action with the Serbs. We paid -- yes, we've already said all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, look now at what Mr. -- President Tudjman said. He seemed to say that the fighting against the Muslims must stop.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did he say so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because Alija Izetbegovic keeps -- well, of course you would have to read all of it, because only if you read the whole will you see the truth, but because of the time constraints we're breaking this down, but one should read all the transcripts from A to Z. He hopes that the Muslims will stop, and I say that they will stop once their offensive is routed, because for as long as they thought that they would beat us, they did not stop, and I state that loud and clear in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean that Mr. Tudjman did not assess the situation on the ground properly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation on the ground was what it was, but he believed Mr. Izetbegovic at his word, although in these transcripts he says again and again that Mr. Izetbegovic says one thing and does another. And despite all that, he had agreements with him and believed him, and Izetbegovic just sold him a lot of lies. There was talk about the harbour, giving the port over to them for a hundred years and so on, but he wants it to stop and makes concessions to have that stop, and the more concessions he makes, the more aggressive they become.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 20 you seem to say that in order to appease tensions with the Muslims, they should start a war against the Serbs. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is that on? Is it the same page, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, look. It's on page 20. Mention is made of -- well, Susak spoke and said that it might be necessary to fight against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what Susak says, Your Honour. He says quite the opposite, in fact, that we can't forget about the Serbs and that the spirit of the agreement signed with Alija Izetbegovic is such, and that it didn't mean any kind of unification, and that it didn't mean that we were now going to go to war against the Serbs. So quite the reverse. It didn't mean that we were going to go to war against the Serbs, and that the union with the Muslims was not established in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
