utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Susak said that, you mentioned the fact that it might be the right time to start a war against the Serbs to ease tensions with the Muslims. Look at what the text says before.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the conditional tense here used. You have to bear in mind, Your Honour, that this is the transcription of a speech. But anyway, the conditional is used here. A year ago I said that we thought we couldn't talk to the Serbs at all, no common ground with the Serbs at all. Now we have reached some sort of negotiation level with the Serbs. And then it's the conditional tense. "I suppose we should now begin a war with the Serbs to alleviate the situation with the Muslims." And we're -- in order to turn things round, you need time. You can't say to your troops, "We're going against the Serbs now, and then we're going to go against the Muslims now. " That's impossible. You need time, that the agreement signed with Alija to sink in. Alija asked us to attack the Serbs straight away. Well, that's not how you do things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are to understand this correctly, there was a form of "cooperation" with the Serbs, but as regarded certain combat areas, you fought the Serbs. So this was a rather complex situation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were you able to work your way round this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, Your Honour: We had dead and wounded in Kiseljak and Vares. We say we'll treat -- they'll say, "We'll treat them at the hospital in Ilidza, and we'll make out the bill as if they were being treated in Switzerland, and you pay for that." And then it says -- we say we need three trucks of ammunition, and then the price for that was so much fuel. So you provide the quantity of fuel they needed. They needed fuel, we need what we needed. So that's what I asked for. And if I'm to blame, then I take the blame on me, because the Serbs weren't defined as enemies as far as I was concerned. The enemy was the side attacking us, and we were there defending ourselves. So neither this Tribunal nor anybody else proclaimed the Serbs to be the aggressors. The Serbs are a people, an ethnic group, and somebody is attacking there, but it's not the HVO. The HVO is not doing the attacking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this last series of documents we will look at P06454. Pages 49, 50, and 51. And then we would look at page 55.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the previous document, we should -- it should read, I suppose that now the war against the Serbs ought to start, or something along those lines to go back to the previous document. But, yes, I am aware of this document. I have it on my screen. I'm know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... familiar with this document. It seems that you are criticising the equipment and the staff of the HVO and Herceg-Bosna and you are going to discuss the military situation in certain areas of the ABiH, and you seem to conclude on page 55 that it is impossible to contend with two enemies at once. Do you remember having said this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I remember it all, from the beginning, that the structures should have been centralised, that the operationalisation was weak, and so on and so forth. I can sign my name to everything it says, that they attacked us in Konjic and all the rest of it. So I subscribe to all that. It's everything that I did indeed say. And then I go on to say that the international public did not accept the fact that the Muslims can be criminals. Of course, at the time everybody was in favour of the Muslims, and now books are appearing saying something quite different. But anyway, here it says that the Muslims were expelled by the Serbs and created ethnic occupation and that the ratio of the population changed from 1:3 to 1:10 to their advantage, and you can find this in any books written internationally. This is a very good analysis on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, look at page 55. You call into question UNPROFOR, and you are saying that UNPROFOR is helping the Muslims to take territories. This is a serious allegation. What did you rely on to say this at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On knowledge, Your Honour. Whether this is a serious accusation or serious allegation or whatever, it's true. Not all UNPROFOR units, but many did help the Muslims, both the English and -- as to the units who were from -- which were from the Islamic countries, that was more or less quite overt, and I know, although the Germans didn't have their units, I do know that they smuggled weapons. In addition to us smuggling weapons to the Muslims through humanitarian. Well, it's very complicated, but I stand by my position here. And they were especially helped by false information, by disseminating false information about what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you were talking about arms trafficking. There are in all institutions bad eggs, without these individuals discrediting the entire organisation. There is a difference, of course. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not everyone engaged in that. There were individuals, but there were also whole structures, entire structures. The Ukrainian, Russians to the Serbs, the Islamic countries to the Muslims, the English, and so on and so forth. And then after that the Americans allowed Iranian planes to land, Turkish planes. Let's not be led astray here. The fact that they want to show that they didn't do what they did and that we are a group of criminals that engendered the war, I state here and now that that is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that this would be the last document, but I would like to show another one. P08066. Page 20. It's a long time after that. The date is the 14th of March, 1994. This is a meeting which was organised seemingly as part of a conference in Vienna. There are prominent figures, Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Granic, Mr. Zubak, Mr. Sanader, and other elected officials and you. This is on page 20. And crucial political issues are being addressed. Questions about international organisations and the European Union. I have two questions. Maybe you had been pardoned at the time, because you attend a very high-level meeting in this case. So if you had been rehabilitated and if you belonged again to the political apparatus, so we know that you left on the 8th of November. You were sidelined for a while, and when did you -- were you appointed to a high-level position again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah. I don't know. For a time they asked me upon my return to put the archive in order so that the documents should be saved, and then I tried to do my best to put the papers in order, three dimensional ones, and to save them, safeguard them. And then Dr. Tudjman called me and asked me to be his military advisor. So that's what I did for a time. Then again he asked me, since we were losing the information battle, he asked me to set up an agency which would unite propaganda and the truth about our positions on Bosnia-Herzegovina and so on. But that didn't succeed. That wasn't successful because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to address the contents of this document. This would take us too far. It seems that there were discussions involving politics, and you took part in these discussions. This enables me to understand how competent you were. You seemed to be -- you seem to have a very good understanding of political matters. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all I wish to know. We shall now move on to other documents which are the presidential transcripts. These were on my list number 7. To display the document, I'm going to ask the registrar to show it to us on the screen and give him the page number. The first document is P00037. What I'm interested in is page 5. You did not attend this meeting. Since you seem to have a good knowledge of political affairs, I feel entitled to put you this question. On page 5 President Tudjman takes the floor. He states that with a view to seeing Croatia being totally independent or independent as part of an alliance, the current borders of Croatia as they were set after World War II were absurd from administrative, commercial, and for a security standpoint. He seems to be saying that according to him, the solution would be to have Bosnia-Herzegovina partitioned. This would serve the interests of Serbia as well as the interests of Croatia. And he adds the Muslim component would have to accept this solution. If we read Mr. Tudjman's statement, it seems that in 1991, on the 8th of June, he is in favour of a partition which would suit Serbia and Croatia. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. I wouldn't agree. I think that this document should be read to the end of it. As I was reading it, I made some notes on the margin. He's talking about Yugoslavia as an alliance of sovereign states. He speaks about the meetings of the six presidents of republics. He says that Bosnia-Herzegovina will be the key, and he says if they go -- goes in a democratic direction, then it's okay for Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, is -- if Serbia takes one part of big then it's a different thing. And now 150947, which is the next page I would like us to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be very precise, look at page -- pages 38 and 39. 39 because it's the bottom of page 38 and the top of page 39 that we need to look at. Let me check whether this is on the screen. The words he uses are quite precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just help the general. The ERN number is 01509447.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tudjman says that there should be equal -- it should be equally interesting for Serbia and Croatia, and the Muslims will have no other solution than to accept this. This is what he says: "This solution is not an easy one to come to, but it is essential." In June of 1991, at any rate, he settles the Muslim question according to what he says here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to what he says here, yes, but look, and let me quote. First he starts by talking about -- well, no. You can't, unfortunately. Your Honours, we can't proceed like this. We can't interpret a speech by a president in this way. He says that there was a joint proposal by Izetbegovic and Gligorov on the table. According to that proposal, they were to create an asymmetric federation -- or a confederation, rather. And in that, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia and Serbia and Montenegro would constitute a federation, and on the other hand Slovenia and Croatia would constitute a confederation with the four states in that federation. And then he goes on to say -- the president says: "I'm sure that in that sense that they're not going to change their viewpoint. If they're not going to change their viewpoint and if they want to lead Bosnia and Herzegovina to Yugoslavia, then he goes on to say then the solution is in the delineation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if we achieve this, then we can look for a potential basis for an alliance of sovereign republics and states. What is being put forth here are various options tabled by certain people at different meetings, how to organise Yugoslavia in order to avoid a war, and what is referred to here is the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as you are concerned, Mr. Tudjman did not have any idea of partition in mind as a solution.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And let me tell you what he says further on, and I quote: "In any case, or after all, in our statements we said that we are in favour of an association with those republics that accept the principles -- all principles ranging from human rights and economic relations and so on which may be the starting point of such an association or a community." Your Honour, we're still speaking of a confederal Yugoslavia here, not about the disintegration. We are still in a confederal Yugoslavia. And what Franjo Tudjman is offering is this: If we reach an agreement on human rights of minorities and on economic relations, there's no reason for us not to stay in that confederal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see whether what you are saying is corroborated by the next document, P00108. I would like page 48 to be displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, I'm sorry that we don't have the rest of that speech to see that Franjo Tudjman quotes the European Union that supported Yugoslavia, and he quotes Markovic, and he says that America is also trying as hard as they can to support Yugoslavia. It is not possible to draw conclusions on sentences which have been singled out from the context. I know this document by heart. I know what happened then and there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since you know all this back to front and since I have spent a lot of time on these presidential transcripts, this will make everybody's task easier. Let me see whether page 48 is on the screen. On page 48, Mr. Tudjman -- well, this is a meeting dated the 8th of January, 1992, and Mr. Tudjman says that Europe, like the rest of the world, would be -- seemed to be in favour of a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina between Croatia and Serbia to avoid the creation of an Islamic state in Europe. For -- the problem which Mr. Tudjman seems to be highlighting is the creation of an Islamic state. The solution would then be to divide or partition the country. This is what he says.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He quotes F. I don't know what F told him. And he also relates what we would hear all the time from western emissaries, and that was their fear from Izetbegovic and his possible Muslim state, but Franjo Tudjman says I believe that we are facing a problem here. Your Honour, you cannot begin to understand how many people were out there trying to impose different solutions on us. Yugoslavia, no Yugoslavia; federation, confederation; Muslim states, no Muslim states. All of these people purported to be representatives of different governments, and Tudjman says: No, this is a problem for us. What is the reality vis-a-vis both of these nations, both nations, the Serbs and the Muslims and where do we stand? What are we supposed to do? All the transcripts here talk about the pain we all suffered to see the light at the end of the tunnel of that chaos, and that's why he kept on repeating and hammering on. Our principles, our politics, did not allow us to opt for anything but what we put our signatures on, and that was for a Bosnia and Herzegovina with the three constituents -- constituent peoples in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As part of the talks in which Zvonko Lerotic will take part on page 53, Lerotic will say at some point that it was possible to envisage the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a recognition de facto of a Serbian state and a Croatian state in Bosnia-Herzegovina that had sovereignly decided to unite. So one of the attendees at the meeting throws this out and puts this forward as an idea of his. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I say or think? Lerotic says here that Muslim has to make decisions in the part where they are, that things should be prepared in political and legal terms. These are simply various and possible options. However, the essence of the matter here again is how to avoid war. What would be the best political solution that would be accepted by the three sides, and no such solution was ever found, and it was never found because the other two peoples wanted different things for themselves and favoured different political options. Only the Croats advocated the right political solution. There were three peoples living there, they were constituent peoples, and that's the kind of documents we signed. And you can't even begin to imagine how many do-gooders from all over the world came to try and impose things on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at our next document, P00130. I would like page 73 to be displayed. This is a meeting which was held on the 3rd of March, 1992. Susak is there, Milas, Cermak, Bobetko, Perkovic, Karlovic, Adanic, Numi Vranje [phoen], Mijatomic [phoen], Tudjman, Zuzul. On page 73 Susak takes the floor and he says that Herzegovina included the area of Herceg-Bosna and Bosanska Posavina. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ERN number is 0186-4040.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0186-4040.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got it. Repeat, please? 6400.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 64040. The last three digits, 040.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 040.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can't find the document, it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it now, thank you. Nothing. He's talking about a region. Somebody mentioned Herzegovina -- Herzegovina, and then he says, "I believe that they believe," and I don't know who he's referring to. I should check. He's talking about Herceg-Bosna and Bosnian Posavina. These are just terms, and he's talking about the defence of Bosnian Posavina and Herceg-Bosna. I don't see anything that I should actually -- he's basically focusing on the problems that he is having with the Croatian army officers, because they are preventing him from arming the people down there for the war that had already started. He's talking about a region. All the Bosnian Posavina at that time was still not part of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the way you interpret what Mr. Susak said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly, Your Honour, what was happening at the time and why I 24 had to be sent down there. The Serb attack was under way. They were killing, 25 destroying Mostar, and Gojko Susak had -- we had a problem with arming the 1 few people who wanted to fight down there, with defending ourselves. At that moment it was just a matter of life and death. There was no talk about Herceg-Bosna or any other regions, no names were mentioned or if they were, they were not important at all. The essence of the matter was the rest of the issue, how to create a command of sorts that would help the population to defend themselves at least on the Neretva River and then further afield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the next document, P00134. Page 115. This meeting was held on the 10th of March, 1992. The attendees were Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Boban, Mr. Krpina, but Mr. Mesic was not at the meeting. Tudjman said this: He said that he spoke to Mr. Izetbegovic, and he says that according to him, a Muslim-Croat Bosnia and Herzegovina should emerge. So this gives the impression that he is in favour of a Muslim Croatian entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as you can see, Boban speaks straight after him, and he seems to endorse the idea. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I've been telling this all the time. We made offers to the Muslims. We told them -- here Mate Boban says, for example, Europe has accepted our principles for establishing peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our principles and our policies. That's what was said from the outset, because we signed, Mate and the others, a principal position on the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina when we were with Cutileiro, but then the situation changed when Serbs took 70 percent, and then Mr. Izetbegovic said, okay, let's allow the Serbs go to their own ghetto and let us create a Croat-Muslim state. And everybody agrees to that. And then we give to the army everything the army needs, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It becomes stronger, and then they pay us the good favour back by hitting us on the head. And Mate Boban went berserk with that situation that changed day in and day out. What person wouldn't go crazy with that, with the time and time again that the international community and Alija Izetbegovic changed their positions? But those were the starting points. This was what was drafted from the outset, the principles that would apply to our policy vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina and then the internal organisation that became part of Cutileiro's plan with one kilometre here, one kilometre there, plus or minus, but that really didn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You make me see what Tudjman said just at the top of the screen. He said, "But these groups are against such policies, and I think that is absurd." When Boban said this, which group was he thinking of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I believe that you're talking about that group which was a group of renegades. I believe that among them -- I don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you precisely, but there was, in any case, a group of Croats, the intellectuals in Sarajevo which advocated -- because in that situation could not -- they didn't dare say anything else. They advocated a unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina that we were against, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, as to this theory of the double discourse as alleged by the Prosecution in their submissions, we have this in March 1992, a meeting, a select committee of people who know each other, and there is Tudjman and Boban. When these men are speaking together, do they have this double game? Are they two-faced, knowing that 15 years down the lane there are going to be Judges scrutinising all this or is what they said true to form, true to reality, that is that Europe was accepting the principles that peace had to be made and it was to be made through this Muslim-Croatian state in Bosnia and Herzegovina? What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is an absurd dilemma to have people in a closed meeting producing documents that should never see day of light in our state or even in yours. Could you imagine such people saying once we die these people would be provided to the world against the law, and we hear or are envisaging that this will happen, that there will be a tribunal, that we will die, we will be outlawed, and let's prevent all that by lying. Please. This is a speculation. This is absurd. And besides, Your Honours, you cannot play a double game with somebody who you keep on arming all that time. It's impossible, impossible, impossible. If you are trying to defeat an enemy, you cannot keep on arming that enemy throughout the entire war. It just doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have another document in which we can see the same problem from two sides. P00167. First let's have page 6, and then let's have page 7.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here's page 6. This meeting was held on the 20th of April, 1992, with Ambassador Warren Zimmerman and other foreign representatives, and people such as Mr. Greguric. On page 6, Tudjman recalled that Croatia had recognised the independence and sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He says, "We recognise the independence ..." et cetera. So this is what he said to the ambassador; is that right? Good. Let's go to page 7.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here -- I apologise, Your Honour, but here he says again the viewpoints of Croatia are very clear and based on principles, and so on and so forth, but you are the one who are asking questions and I am supposed to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So Mr. Tudjman claims before the American ambassador that they have recognised its independence. Fine. Now let's move to page 7. At the very top of it. And this is what he said: He said that the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina had asked him not to give up the territory that belonged to Croatia prior to the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... uncertain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So isn't there a problem here in relation to what he's just said before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Prior to that he said that Croatia maintains principles and views. It had recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina, and of course that people who had been tortured and beaten up by the Serbs came to Franjo Tudjman and told him let's secede from Bosnia-Herzegovina if we are going to defend that part, and he told them you can't do that. He told them we have to strive for a political solution. We cannot -- the Serbs want to secede is what he's saying. We cannot copy them. We can't do the same as they do. We have to look for a political solution. I'm talking about a certain number of people. He says that there are such people. And second of all, he says that he told them that this would amount to nothing. Thirdly, he says that he recognises Bosnia and Herzegovina. And his -- he pursued that same policy based principles until the very end. There were a lot of pressures by the international community talking about three states, cantons, federation, confederation, and so on and so forth. But, for example, on P00167, page -- he says the same thing, and I quote: "Here I would only say that the conditions -- or preconditions," if you will, "which we present in a letter sent to Secretary Baker, are very important for us, very significant for us, because we're talking about the OSC [as interpreted] principles and the principles which we hope will govern us -- by which we will be governed in our behaviour not only in our mutual relations but in our multilateral relations." In other words, Franjo Tudjman recognises the OSCE, which implies that no borders could be changed by force. And I'm repeating this: We should read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have P00336 now. We'll first have a look at page 42 and then move to page 49, where there may be a variation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the last four digits is 32 -- 3251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For everybody to follow, this was held on the 21st of July, 1992. It was a very long meeting. It started at midday and ended at 10.15 in the evening. Ten-hour long meeting. Izetbegovic, Pelivan, Zuzul, Greguric, Granic attended among others. On page 42, Tudjman speaks to Izetbegovic and says this: "Mr. Izetbegovic, the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia are not in danger," et cetera. So this sentence seems to show that Tudjman reassures Izetbegovic in saying that there's not going to be any shift in borders. What do you think.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. And not only that. I don't know why you skipped the beginning where he says that Croatia is under threat from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and so on. Throughout this text, in the whole of it, reference is made exclusively to Bosnia-Herzegovina and how -- well, it says deal with the position of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia-Herzegovina was never questioned or challenged either in the policy of Herceg-Bosna or Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to the -- to page 43. We see Tudjman who keeps on speaking, and I think that the words he then utters are very important. Here they are on page 43. At the very beginning he said this: "We have recognised and the international community stands by it. So this is one of the reasons why we have fully supported the Croatian people when they voted in the referendum ..." So Tudjman tells Izetbegovic that when the Croats voted for the referendum, they voted for the recognition of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is this a correct analysis by Tudjman, and did you have the same analysis at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both. And that's precisely what I'm saying here. The Republic of Croatia was recognised, and now he's trying to persuade and intensively advocate a referendum for the Croats and enable, through the Badinter Commission, for -- enable Bosnia-Herzegovina to become an independent state. Had we not gone out to a referendum it wouldn't have become an independent state, and so not only the speeches but everything else has been conceived to take a portion of -- out of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Oh, come on, I don't think even anthropoid monkeys would do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're too fast.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes that's right, I'll slow down. But that's something that one can just cannot understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see what Izetbegovic will say later, because we realise that this is a much more complex problem. Let's have a look at page 49. The last line of the page. Can the usher show it to us? Thank you. The last four words are by Mr. Izetbegovic, and they seem to be important. He says: "One individual, one vote." He recalls this principle. And let's move straight away to page 50, then I'll ask my question. But first let's go to page 50. Izetbegovic is still speaking. Look at the second line. He speaks about Central Bosnia. Remember what he said, one individual, one vote. And now he said this: "For example, the HVO in Central Bosnia is now trying to take over the power in the areas where 20 to 30 percent of the inhabitants are Croats while 60 to 70 percent are Muslims." So first he started with this principle of one individual, one vote. Then he said that there were areas where Croats are -- were in a minority and wanted to take power. So is this not the substantial problem?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Izetbegovic here is presenting a basic problem, the basic problem for his war option -- or of his war option. That's what this situation is. Now, Your Honours, to be quite clear, in all these negotiations, talks, transcripts, well, I don't know where they used it, but it was recorded in one of the transcripts where I say "expel," but I'll speak slowly. The word that I used there was the only word for which I claim that it was written outside my -- beyond my style, beyond my gestures, just that one word. Now, this is ethnic occupation. This is not information based on a population census, Your Honours. These figures and -- these facts and figures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Praljak, but I would like to -- to draw your attention to the continuation of that transcript which our President has asked us to look at, and after words where there is a reference to Central Bosnia, then Izetbegovic continues and I quote: "Let us say that they can achieve that -- I mean the, trying to take over the power in the areas where 20 to 30 percent of inhabitants are Croats, and 60 to 70 percent are Muslims." And then he continues that: "They can achieve that," he means the Croats, I believe, "because they are armed or got an assistance from Croatia, and we already have rifles and they actually have machine-guns, mortars, et cetera. So let it say that it can be done." Let me then end the quotation. And so my question is that do you think that Izetbegovic, to put it very bluntly, lied when he said this or he had something really substantial to say on which he was able to state this position of his? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's lying. Izetbegovic is lying here. First he received cannons in the joint distribution from the Bratstvo factory. At that time he had tanks, and he had helicopters. He also received weapons from Croatia. Second, in the population census of 1991, the area of Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Kiseljak, the majority population was Croatian or mostly. Now, what Mr. Izetbegovic here says was the result of the fact that the Serbs had expelled the Muslims and because they occupied the territory in ethnic terms. And now he says, "Here we are. This is how things stand. There are 60 or 70 percent of us. One man, one vote, and you can take yourself off and I won't tell you where." And it would have a lovely -- it would resound beautifully in Hungarian if I could use the Hungarian terms of where to send someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I know what you mean. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And precisely this one man, one vote, from the Islamic declaration onwards, is what caused the war between the Croats and the Muslims, precisely that. And I would go to war tomorrow for that thesis. It's my land, my territory, and nobody's going to occupy me ethnically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to page 51. Izetbegovic gave the example of Travnik. At the very beginning of the page he said that the Muslims were the majority in Travnik, and in spite of that they're trying to impose on them a new authority. So this is what Izetbegovic said. What do you think of that? And you know very well what the situation was like in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Izetbegovic his -- is lying before everybody's eyes. Well, you had a trial here. What Croatian authority in Travnik? They killed us like -- slaughtered us like kittens. They expelled us, captured us, mistreated us. The 7th and 17th Muslim did all kinds of things there. But let me tell you, 0186-3253 is the page I'd like to refer to, and it's Franjo Tudjman speaking. No, it's 3254, the page number. Mr. Izetbegovic -- he says to Mr. Izetbegovic, and I quote: "Croatia was the side which had a principled relationship towards the territorial whole and entity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, Croatia has taken the principled position in the sense of -- in that sense, that you," and you means Alija Izetbegovic, "you in the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina should also consider and take into consideration the practical situation of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina." But Alija Izetbegovic is not going to take that into consideration, the situation of the Croatian people. He doesn't want to do that. He says one man, one vote. And the fact that the Serbs expelled us and there are 30.000 of us more in Mostar today, well, there'll be peace and we'll take it and make the state that he said they would make in the Islamic declaration. Tricks. They're all tricks. Lies, duplicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us return to page 51, because something is said about the Banovina which may be of interest. Can you see? We can see that Mr. Tudjman in the presence of Mr. Izetbegovic recalls the Banovina of 1939. And then he seems to be telling Izetbegovic -- it says the interest of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia is to have friendly relations. So my impression, and I'd like you to confirm it, Mr. Praljak, my impression is that Tudjman tries to make Izetbegovic understand that there is the issue of Banovina but that he actually seeks to -- friendly relations with the Muslims. Is this the right interpretation or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely in that way, Your Honour. When Franjo Tudjman or we speak about a Banovina, the Banovina is there because in that area of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time the majority population was Croatian. It wasn't given because there were Frenchmen there or the English. The Serbs let it go after a lot of effort. So in that sense he's speaking as an historian. He says, "We're experiencing a fall, but we want to have friendly relations with Bosnia-Herzegovina, but first settle relations with the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina; you, the authorities in Sarajevo, that is."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Izetbegovic to understand the problem properly, it seems that he is telling him what can you do without Ploce and his connections. Does he want Mr. Izetbegovic to understand that he needs an outlet on the sea, and all of this requires a friendly relationship and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little differently. First of all, he's offering him something. Then he says, "Mr. Izetbegovic, it's difficult for you without Croatia." Then you gave Ploce later on and everything. You have your outlet at Ploce. What Western Herzegovina? Croatia is your outlet. So he's trying to instill reason into Izetbegovic, and quite frankly, Your Honours, I wouldn't have done it that way. I would have done it a little differently and said it differently. I would say, "Gentlemen, there's a sovereign nation over there and you're going to behave towards them in the corresponding way or we're going to switch the taps off." But Tudjman was cooperative. He wanted to be cooperative. He says, "Here, you have an outlet. Here's the port. Here's Ploce. Here's recognition. Here's everything." And in return he never received any guarantees from the man, none at all. Izetbegovic never ever said what kind of Bosnia and Herzegovina he'd like to see except in the Islamic declaration. Find me another document, you won't find it. No proposal in any other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To get back to the Banovina, let's look at page 61. Here we have it. Look at the top. Tudjman mentions the Banovina again and discusses it with Mr. Izetbegovic. He says that there would be 98 to 99 percent of Croats living there. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't interpret that in the right way. Once again, this is full cooperation on Franjo Tudjman's part. He says we're not asking for everyone, that is to say the Croats, to be in a canton of some kind. What we're asking for is that those areas, those territories, which have become constituted and which were in part within the frameworks of the Croatian Banovina, that that should be a sort of Croatian canton. And he says, well, there's this awareness and compactness. Western Herzegovina is ethnically 99 percent Croatian, so why prevent it from having a cantonal type of organisation, organised according to a canton? And then he says Izetbegovic, what is it in fact that you want? At the same time, Franjo Tudjman is offering districts and cultural autonomy to Croatian Serbs, who are a national minority, and here, he is begging Izetbegovic to give a constituent people, a sovereign people, the right to their own canton. So you see how he is grovelling before this man. Franjo Tudjman is grovelling and down on his knees in front of this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... says after that he seems to agree to the fact that in this area the Croats are in the majority, around a hundred percent. And then he reminds him of the situation in Central Bosnia, and he says there it's all mixed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we've said several times here. Alija Izetbegovic always offered Franjo Tudjman -- he said take Herzegovina. Take Western Herzegovina and take it away. Carry it off. So you saw with Okun and Klein generals -- well, Izetbegovic offered Franjo Western Herzegovina. He said take it to Croatia whereas where the population was mixed, you leave that to me, he says. So following on from that principle, Your Honours, if you have a nation which is 49.9 percent of the population and the other is 51 percent of the population, then he would have implemented what he wanted. That is to say, an Islamic republic. They're mixed, the population's mixed he says. Well, they're mixed everywhere. The population is mixed everywhere, but not a 50/50 ratio. And apart from that, Franjo Tudjman said several times, Okay. Well, there'll be equal rights. You can't put any nation in a subjugated position in terms of national rights, ethnic rights, but he says we're mixed, we've occupied this ethnically, now leave it to us, and you can take Western Herzegovina. Well, a little more than -- that won't be the case. Yes, I'll start from the beginning. I have to go back a bit. I don't know how far you understand this, but it's so clear that Alija Izetbegovic, with all these offers made from Franjo Tudjman and understanding that he was a cooperative man, he says here you've got -- Here, take Western Herzegovina and do what you will, but everywhere elsewhere where we're a mixed population. It will be one man one vote, there are more of us and then we'll act in the way I described it in the Islamic declaration. No, that was not what was going to happen, because before the ethnic occupation there was a relative Croatian majority in Novi Travnik, in Vitez, in Busovaca, Kiseljak. I think in Vares as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, you're going too fast. Slow down. You quote five places in a split second. Please slow down, Mr. Praljak. I know that you want to tell us a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll check that out by Monday because I have a book with all the statistical data, but the majority population, not in absolute terms but in relative terms, as far as I remember that was no Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Vitez, Kiseljak, Vares, and so on. For the ethnic occupation that the Muslims enforced once they were expelled by the Serbs. And that's the essential point here. Alija Izetbegovic realises full well that he won't be able to bring the Muslims back from the territories they've been expelled from because he's not going to defeat the Serbs, be able to defeat the Serbs. So the BH Army did not fight against the Serbs at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will stop with documents, because we have just about reached 6.00. On Monday we will have a look at 15 or so presidential transcripts, and after that I will look at a document that states that the commander needs to seize the military prosecutor, and then this will be the end of my questions. I will address all the documents you have mentioned in your submissions you filed in April. There are quite a lot of these. I hope I will be able to finish on Monday. Otherwise, we will finish on Tuesday. I hope we can finish on Monday. Once I have finished I don't know who will begin on the side of the Defence, and Defence counsel you need to prepare your cross-examination which will start next week. At this juncture, could you tell me who is going to start?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the moment we haven't got a firm agreement as to which Defence team will kick off, but we'll certainly know that by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a few days to reach an agreement on this. Let me remind you that you have 50 percent of Praljak's time. Since he has testified for 40 hours, you have 20 hours, which is a lot of time. I hope you will be able to use your 20 hours. Mr. Praljak, I hope you're not too tired. You will be able to continue on Monday, will you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not too tired. I can carry on for another year and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish you all a pleasant evening and we shall resume on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of June, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
